title: If you want to play around - You can fully rebuild retro games with AI in 24h
author: llothar
selftext:
Just so you know, at least with Opus 5.5 you can give it any retro game and it will happily decompile it and reimplement it for you, for example in Godot. 

I did that with Space Federation / Star Reach. in 24h I had a confirmed pixel perfect copy. Later in 30 minutes it gave me fully working Android version. It literally took 5 minutes of my time.

I had [claude.md](http://claude.md) file with:



`# Information`



`This is a project to replicate the game Space Federation / Star Reach. This is an old DOS game with source code long gone.`



`1. Keep an up to date Wiki files with relevant information, bugs, features, status, etc.`

`2. Install whatever needs installing to make this work`

`3. First focus on fully recreating the game.` 

`4. After the replication is done, focus on adding modern features like custom screen resolution, higher resolution assets etc.`

`5. The game is to run on modern systems, Linux and Windows.`

  
Thats it. There were 2 minor bugs that came out in my testing. I also asked it to go through the decompiled files to ensure all functionality is ported.

  
It worked like magic. I then added higher resolution, better mouse support, HD sprites with additional angles (upscale, gaussian splatting, render additional angles, downscale).

I later tested same approach with Big Red Racing - this was a bit more testing, but also gave me fully playable ported game within 24 hours.

  
You can do whatever you want. Need For Speed with fancy lighting and multiplayer over internet? Sure. On Android? Yup. It is stupid simple.

  
Until now projects like OpenTTD, OpenRA, or OpenLoco took years to make. Now it is literally 24 hours and costs like a fifth of your Claude subscription.

replies.author: LucidFir
replies.body:
You obviously couldn't reproduce actual No Man's Sky, but you could make something recognizably No Man's Sky-like while remaining genuine Tetris:
Space: mostly empty well; your ship is a persistent arrangement of blocks. Incoming pieces/garbage represent asteroids, pirates and destinations.
Planets: landing changes the interpretation of the board. The existing pile becomes procedurally generated terrain.
Walking: instead of the world scrolling normally, pieces are inserted/removed so terrain moves around a little block-character.
Mining: completing particular shapes/lines removes terrain and gives resources.
Procedural generation: a seed determines biome, terrain patterns, hazards and resources.
Inventory: literally another little Tetris packing problem.
Crafting: arrange resources into prescribed polyomino shapes.
Ship upgrades: permanently alter your ship's block pattern or what pieces you're allowed to manipulate.
Galaxy: each completed/escaped board generates the seed for another system.
Death: hilariously and appropriately, topping out.
And I'd impose one important rule: every visible thing must ultimately be made from actual Tetris cells and every important player action must correspond to legal Tetris-piece manipulation. Otherwise we're just making a pixel-art game that looks like Tetris.
So you'd have this absurd progression:
Tetris → mine resources → build ship → launch → fly through block-space → discover procedurally generated Tetris planet → land → explore → mine → upgrade → launch → next procedural system.
That could actually be made. And unlike “No Man's Sky but with Tetris graphics,” the constraint could make it genuinely interesting.
If you want, I can build a tiny playable proof-of-concept directly in this chat to see whether the idea actually works.

comments.body: When UE7 comes out, remaking Skyrim in it but with a bunch of mods already baked into the pipeline for the visuals would be incredible. Leave it extensible for Oblivion and Morrowind content to be added in as well. I love TES but god do I hate how unoptimized the Creation Engine truly is as someone who has spent thousands of hours building mods for the game, thousands more applying them to the game, and less than a thousand playing the game because it would never run as smooth as I wanted it to (though came close with my last attempt thanks to the Community Shaders team.) comments.author: Wide-Director-2398
comments.body:
I've been doing something very similar with Band-Kun, a pretty obscure Japanese PC-98 / FM Towns game from 1990.

https://preview.redd.it/mh91asck92th1.png?width=640&format=png&auto=webp&s=1da6a9ad3aa0c472ca2da686a4f33e5b58693a1f

I used AI to help decompile and rebuild the game as a modern application that can run without emulation. The first goal was just to reproduce the original game correctly and make its data and structure accessible again.

But I think the really interesting part starts after that.

Once an old game has been decompiled, rebuilt and its structure is open again, you don't necessarily need AI anymore. It basically becomes a game you can mod normally.

In my case I've been manually adding new systems: time and opening hours, rent, band morale, concerts, recording sessions, record releases, royalties, record collecting, new music, etc.

I'm also working on tools to create completely new scenarios, with new cities, characters, graphics, music and data. So the reconstructed game becomes more like an engine for making new content.

I think this is one of the most interesting uses of AI for old games. Not necessarily generating the game or its content with AI, but using AI to get through the huge reverse engineering barrier and make an old closed game editable again.

After that, people can draw new graphics, compose music, write scenarios, research historical content, code new mechanics, or mod the game in the usual way.

My project is here if anyone is curious:  
[https://band-kun-unlimited.onrender.com/](https://band-kun-unlimited.onrender.com/)

The site may take a little while to load the first time. I don't have a VPS yet, so it's currently running on a free hosting service that goes to sleep when nobody is using it.
